steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Prosocial behaviour is any act that benefits others. Altruism is helping with no expectation of personal gain - the debate is whether true altruism exists or whether all helping is ultimately self-serving.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: The bystander effect: people are less likely to help when others are present. Latane & Darley's (1968) smoke experiment: 75% helped when alone vs 10-38% when in a group.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Diffusion of responsibility: in a group, each person assumes someone else will help. This was famously linked to the murder of Kitty Genovese (1964), where 38 witnesses allegedly did nothing - though later accounts question this version.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: The cost-reward model (Piliavin): people weigh up the costs of helping against the rewards. If costs outweigh rewards, people are less likely to help. This model suggests helping is always rational and self-interested.

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Describe the bystander effect and explain why the presence of others reduces helping behaviour. | Evaluate whether true altruism exists, using psychological research. | Explain how the cost-reward model accounts for prosocial behaviour and evaluate its limitations.

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: More bystanders = LESS helping. This is the bystander effect. Diffusion of responsibility: 'Someone else will do it.' Pluralistic ignorance: 'Nobody else seems worried.' Cost-reward model: if COSTS > REWARDS, no helping. If REWARDS > COSTS, helping occurs.
